verifyNote: Written from standard UK anterior eye practice (College of Optometrists, TFOS DEWS II). Always check against Prof Naroo's and Dr Aujla's slides — grading schemes and routines can differ.

topics.title: Slit lamp illumination techniques
topics.summary: Each slit lamp illumination technique shows different things. Start broad (diffuse) to survey, narrow the beam to look at layers and depth (direct focal: parallelepiped, optic section, conical beam), and use indirect methods — indirect illumination, retro-illumination, specular reflection, sclerotic scatter and tangential — for subtle changes.
keyPoints: Diffuse: diffuser in place, wide beam, low magnification (typically 6× or 10×) — overall view of the eye and adnexa.
Optic section (direct): thin beam, low to high magnification — shows depth: AC depth and localising nerve fibres, vessels, infiltrates and cataracts.
Parallelepiped (direct): broader beam lighting a block of cornea — corneal nerve fibres, punctate keratitis.
Conical beam (direct): small circular, short narrow beam at 45–60°, medium magnification, darkened room so the pupil is a dark background (Tyndall effect) — AC cells and flare.
Indirect: look to the side of the beam (decouple the observation system) — epithelial vesicles and erosions, iris pathology, iris sphincter, limbal vessels.

Retro-illumination: light reflected from the iris or fundus, moderately wide beam, decoupled, medium to high magnification — microcysts (appear 'reversed'), vacuoles, lens opacities, CL deposits, vascularisation.
Specular reflection: angle of illumination = angle of observation, medium to high magnification, seen in one eyepiece only — tear film debris and flow, endothelium, lens 'orange peel'.
Sclerotic scatter: 1–1.5 mm slit on the limbus, total internal reflection, observation decoupled and focused on the cornea, low magnification — scars, oedema, corneal foreign bodies.
Tangential: illumination and observation almost at right angles (about 70°), low to medium magnification, wide beam — iris freckles, tumours, general integrity of cornea and iris.
examTraps: Using high magnification for the first look — start with diffuse at low magnification.
Setting conical beam at high magnification in a lit room — it's medium magnification in a darkened room.
Forgetting to decouple for indirect, retro-illumination and sclerotic scatter (you look beside the beam, not at it).
Looking for specular reflection with both eyes — it's only visible through one eyepiece.

diagram.description: Top view of the slit lamp: illumination arm at about 45–60° to the microscope, narrow beam entering the cornea. Inset shows the resulting optic section: a curved bright band through the cornea with tear film, epithelium, stroma and endothelium layers, then the dark anterior chamber and the iris.

goDeeper.heading: Setting up the slit lamp
goDeeper.body: Clean the headrest and chinrest and adjust the table height. With a focusing rod: turn each eyepiece anticlockwise to maximum plus, put the rod in place at the shared axis of the illumination and observation systems, narrow the slit, and turn each eyepiece in turn until the slit is just in focus; then set the IPD, position the patient and adjust the chinrest. Without a rod: position the patient first, then focus on the closed eyelid — rotate the illumination arm and watch the slit; if it moves 'against', move the slit lamp closer; if 'with', move it away; when it doesn't move, the eyelid is at the shared focus and you can focus the eyepieces on the slit, then set the IPD.

goDeeper.heading: Coupled and decoupled
goDeeper.body: Normally the illumination and observation systems are coupled — both focused on the same point, so you look at what the beam lights. For indirect illumination, retro-illumination and sclerotic scatter you decouple them, so the microscope focuses beside the beam. The direct beam can 'bleach' subtle defects from view, which is why looking beside it shows things like epithelial vesicles and erosions better.

goDeeper.heading: Choosing a technique
goDeeper.body: Survey with diffuse. Then ask what you want to know: depth or thickness → optic section; texture of a surface or stroma → parallelepiped; something faint or translucent (microcysts, vacuoles, KPs) → retro-illumination; generalised corneal haze → sclerotic scatter; endothelium or tear film detail → specular; AC cells → conical beam.

goDeeper.heading: Looking for cells and flare
goDeeper.body: Dim the room fully so the pupil acts as a dark background. Use a short, narrow circular beam at about 45–60°, medium magnification, focused in the AC between the cornea and lens. Cells look like dust in a sunbeam; flare looks like a smoky haze (the Tyndall effect, from protein). They're signs of anterior uveitis — grade them and refer as your guidance says.

goDeeper.heading: Specular reflection
goDeeper.body: Focus on the area of interest, then swing the illumination arm until the bright mirror-like reflection (a Purkinje image from the tear film) appears — angle of illumination equals angle of observation. Use medium to high magnification; it's only visible through one eyepiece at a time. Reduce the angle to look at deeper structures such as the endothelium (dark gaps suggest guttata or polymegethism) or the lens surface ('orange peel').

topics.title: Systematic anterior segment examination
topics.summary: A routine order — outside in, front to back — means nothing gets missed: lids and lashes, lid margins, conjunctiva, cornea, tear film, anterior chamber, iris and lens. Do it the same way every time and record both eyes.
keyPoints: Order: lids and lashes → lid margins (meibomian glands) → bulbar and palpebral conjunctiva → limbus → cornea (epithelium, stroma, endothelium) → tear film → AC → iris → lens.
Start each part with diffuse light at low magnification, then go more detailed.
Use fluorescein after the white-light exam (it changes what you see).
Grade findings with a named scale and note location (e.g. 'inferior', 'at 4 o'clock').
Check AC depth (Van Herick) and look for cells/flare when indicated.
Evert the upper lid when the history suggests it (FB sensation, CL wear, itch).
Always compare with the other eye.
examTraps: Jumping straight to the cornea and missing lid margin disease.
Instilling fluorescein before checking the tear film and conjunctiva in white light.
Recording 'normal' without saying what was checked.

diagram.description: Cross-section of the anterior eye labelled from front to back: eyelids with meibomian glands, conjunctiva, limbus, cornea (epithelium, Bowman's layer, stroma, Descemet's membrane, endothelium), anterior chamber, iris, lens.

goDeeper.heading: Lids and lashes
goDeeper.body: Look for lid position (ptosis, entropion, ectropion), lumps (chalazion, stye, papilloma, BCC features), lash direction (trichiasis), crusting, collarettes or cylindrical dandruff at the lash base (Demodex), and the meibomian gland orifices (capping, toothpaste secretions).

goDeeper.heading: Cornea layer by layer
goDeeper.body: Use a parallelepiped to scan the cornea in sections, then optic section to place anything you find: epithelium (punctate staining, microcysts), stroma (scars, infiltrates, oedema), endothelium (guttata, KPs). Note size, depth, location and whether it stains.

goDeeper.heading: Recording
goDeeper.body: Write a line per structure for each eye, e.g. 'Lids/lashes: clear. Conj: bulbar redness 1 (Efron). Cornea: clear, no staining. AC: deep and quiet, VH 4. Iris: NAD. Lens: clear.' Use a drawing for anything abnormal, with size and position.

checklist.title: Anterior eye routine (each eye)
steps: Lids and lashes (diffuse, low mag).

Anterior chamber: Van Herick, cells/flare if indicated.
Iris and pupil margin.
Lens (best through a dilated pupil).
Fluorescein: cornea and conjunctiva under cobalt blue with barrier filter.
Record with grades and drawings.

topics.title: Anterior chamber angle assessment
topics.summary: From Dr Aujla's week 5 lecture: dilating can trigger acute angle closure, so assess the angle first. Van Herick is the routine screen; the pen torch and Smith's method are cruder; imaging gives cross-sections; only gonioscopy shows the angle directly.
keyPoints: Aqueous inflates the eye, feeds the avascular tissues, defends against pathogens and keeps the refractive index; 80–90% drains through the trabecular meshwork, 10–20% by the uveoscleral route.
Acute angle closure: pain, blurred vision with coloured haloes, nausea and vomiting, an emergency. Warn patients before dilating.
Risk factors: shallow chamber, forward or thick lens, small cornea, short eye, steep cornea, age, female sex (4:1) and East Asian ethnicity.

Van Herick: 10–16x, narrow bright slit at 60° temporal, at the limbus; compare peripheral chamber depth with corneal thickness. Grade 4 (1:1 or more, closure impossible), 3 (1:½, unlikely), 2 (1:¼, possible), 1 (under 1:¼, very likely), 0 (closed).
Pen torch: light from the temporal side parallel to the iris; nasal iris in shadow 0/25/50/75/100% gives grades 4 to 0. Very crude.
Smith's method: horizontal 1–2 mm slit at 60°; chamber depth ≈ slit length × 1.4; under 2 mm suggests risk.
Ultrasound, Scheimpflug imaging (Pentacam) and AS-OCT give cross-sections but don't view the angle directly.

Gonioscopy (direct Koeppe or indirect mirror lenses) is the gold standard. Structures front to back: Schwalbe's line, unpigmented and pigmented trabecular meshwork, scleral spur, ciliary body. The superior angle is usually the narrowest.
examTraps: Treating van Herick as a diagnosis rather than a screen.
Saying the inferior angle is the narrowest.
Pressing hard on a corneal gonio lens: it folds Descemet's membrane and can falsely widen the angle.

diagram.description: Slit lamp view of the temporal limbus with a narrow beam. The bright curved band is the corneal section; next to it a dark gap (peripheral AC), then the beam lands on the iris. Four mini panels show grades 4, 3, 2 and 1 with the dark gap getting smaller relative to the corneal band.

goDeeper.heading: Gonioscopy in practice
goDeeper.body: Indications include narrow angles on van Herick (grade 2 or less), glaucoma, pigment dispersion or pseudoexfoliation, neovascular risk, trauma and after iridotomy; not after recent trauma or surgery. Scleral (Goldmann) lenses need coupling fluid; corneal four-mirror lenses (Posner, Zeiss, Sussman) are about 9 mm. Use low magnification with a 2–3 mm parallelepiped, put the mirror opposite the quadrant you want, start inferiorly and grade all 360°.

flashcards.back: About 60° between illumination and microscope (microscope straight ahead).
After recent ocular trauma or recent intraocular surgery.
Pain, blurred vision with coloured haloes, nausea and vomiting.

mcq.explanation: Grade 4 = 1:1 (wide open), grade 3 = 1:½ (open), grade 2 = 1:¼ (narrow), grade 1 = <¼ (dangerously narrow).

topics.title: Fluorescein and lissamine green staining
topics.summary: Sodium fluorescein shows where the corneal (and conjunctival) epithelium is disrupted or missing; lissamine green shows damaged or devitalised cells and mucus, especially on the conjunctiva. Grade staining by location, type and extent with a named scale.
keyPoints: Sodium fluorescein (NaFl): view with a broad beam, cobalt blue light and a yellow (Wratten) barrier filter — cornea, conjunctiva and TBUT. It stains where cell junctions are broken or cells missing and pools in defects.
Look at the cornea soon after instillation, before it diffuses into the stroma.
Lissamine green: view with white light (a red filter helps); best for conjunctival staining; look 1–4 minutes after instillation.
Describe staining: type (punctate, diffuse, coalescent, patch), depth, location (zones or clock hours) and extent.
Grading options: Efron or CCLRU for CL work; Oxford scheme (panels A–E) for dry eye; NEI zones.
Patterns help diagnosis: inferior band (exposure/MGD), superior (SLK, upper lid FB), 3 & 9 o'clock (RGP), dendrite (HSV).
Avoid standard NaFl with soft lenses in situ — it stains them.
examTraps: Viewing fluorescein without the barrier filter and under-grading staining.
Using lissamine green with the cobalt blue light.
Forgetting to look at the conjunctiva as well as the cornea.

diagram.description: Cornea divided into five zones: central circle and four peripheral segments (superior, inferior, nasal, temporal). Example staining dots drawn in the inferior zone, labelled 'inferior punctate staining, grade 1'.

goDeeper.heading: Recognising staining patterns
goDeeper.body: Inferior punctate staining: exposure, incomplete blinking, MGD/evaporative dry eye. Interpalpebral band: dry eye. 3 and 9 o'clock: RGP edge drying. Superior arcuate: tight soft lens or SEAL. Linear vertical scratches: FB under the upper lid — evert it. Dendritic branching ulcer with terminal bulbs: herpes simplex keratitis — refer.

goDeeper.heading: Seidel test
goDeeper.body: If a penetrating injury or wound leak is suspected, paint concentrated fluorescein over the area and watch under cobalt blue. A stream of dilute (bright green) aqueous flowing through the dark orange dye is a positive Seidel — an emergency.

goDeeper.heading: Practical tips
goDeeper.body: Moisten the strip with saline and touch it to the lower conjunctiva (not the cornea); one small drop's worth is plenty. Ask the patient to blink a few times. Too much dye floods the view and makes grading harder.

flashcards.back: Disrupted or missing epithelium (cell junction damage) and pooling in defects.
Damaged/devitalised cells and mucus, especially on the conjunctiva.

topics.title: Tear film assessment
topics.summary: From Dr Dutta's week 8 lecture: know where each tear layer comes from, how blinking and drainage work, and the tests for tear quantity, stability, lipid layer, surface damage and symptoms.
keyPoints: Lipid (0.1–0.2 µm): meibomian glands and glands of Zeis and Moll; reduces evaporation. Aqueous (about 7 µm): main lacrimal gland (reflex) and accessory glands of Krause and Wolfring (basal). Mucin (about 0.05 µm): goblet cells and corneal epithelium; makes the surface wettable.
Volume about 7 µl, produced at 1.2 µl/min, turned over every 5 minutes; open-eye osmolarity about 315 mOsm/kg.
Blink rate about 12/min, raised by conversation, anxiety, tiredness and dry environments, lowered by reading, hard tasks and screens.
Quantity: Schirmer (only useful for comparison), phenol red thread, meniscus height. Stability: fluorescein TBUT (which adds volume) and non-invasive break-up (NIBUT).
Lipid layer: Tearscope interference patterns. Surface damage: fluorescein, rose bengal (dead or degenerate cells and poor mucin cover; irritating) and lissamine green. Symptoms: e.g. OSDI.
Also check tear debris, meniscus shape, lid wiper and meibomian glands. Meibomian gland dysfunction and blepharitis destabilise the lipid layer and cause dry, itchy eyes and lens intolerance.
examTraps: Calling TBUT a secretion test: it measures stability.
Doing fluorescein TBUT before non-invasive tests.

diagram.description: Cross-section of the tear film on the corneal epithelium: outer lipid layer (from meibomian glands), middle aqueous layer (lacrimal gland), inner mucin/glycocalyx layer (goblet cells, epithelium).

goDeeper.heading: Not in the slides: TFOS DEWS II cut-offs
goDeeper.body: Dry eye is diagnosed on symptoms (OSDI ≥ 13 or DEQ-5 ≥ 6) plus at least one sign: NIBUT under 10 s, osmolarity ≥ 308 mOsm/L or an inter-eye difference over 8, or ocular surface staining. A meniscus under about 0.2 mm suggests low volume; Schirmer I of 5 mm or less in 5 minutes is low. Do non-invasive tests first.

cases.scenario: A 55-year-old woman reports gritty, burning eyes and a dry mouth for months. Tear meniscus is low, Schirmer I is 3 mm, and there's interpalpebral fluorescein and lissamine staining.
cases.question: What type of dry eye is this and what else should you consider?
cases.modelAnswer: Aqueous-deficient dry eye with surface damage. Dry mouth raises the possibility of Sjögren's syndrome. Manage symptoms (preservative-free lubricants) and refer to her GP for investigation of a possible systemic cause, following local guidance. Review and record.

topics.title: Lid eversion technique
topics.summary: Everting the upper lid shows the upper tarsal conjunctiva, where foreign bodies hide and where papillae and follicles show up. It's quick and comfortable when done smoothly and explained well.
keyPoints: Prepare the slit lamp first, and explain: it feels strange but shouldn't hurt.
Ask the patient to look down (and keep looking down) throughout.
Use a cotton bud (or your finger); push the lashes apart with the bud if needed.
Hold the upper lashes and pull the lid gently down and away from the eye.
Place the bud at the top of the tarsal plate (about 10 mm above the lid margin).
Fold the lid up over the bud with a 'down and round' motion of the lashes and bud.
Look with white light and with blue light (after fluorescein); to return the lid, ask the patient to look up and blink.
examTraps: Asking the patient to look up during eversion (makes it impossible).
Pressing on the eyeball with the cotton bud.
Forgetting to look with fluorescein — papillae show up much better.

diagram.description: Three-step side view: (1) patient looks down, lashes held, bud placed at the upper border of the tarsal plate; (2) lid folded up over the bud; (3) everted lid held against the brow, showing the tarsal conjunctiva.
labels: Cotton bud at upper tarsal border

goDeeper.heading: Papillae vs follicles
goDeeper.body: Papillae: raised bumps with a central blood vessel, on the tarsal conjunctiva — allergic conjunctivitis, contact lens papillary conjunctivitis, bacterial conjunctivitis. Follicles: pale, avascular lymphoid swellings with vessels around them, often in the lower fornix — viral (adenovirus), chlamydial, some drug reactions.

goDeeper.heading: Foreign bodies
goDeeper.body: A subtarsal FB causes a scratchy feeling and vertical linear corneal staining. It can often be removed with a moistened cotton bud once everted (within your scope and training). Embedded or corneal FBs, or any rust ring, may need referral depending on competence and local arrangements.

checklist.title: Upper lid eversion
steps: Prepare the slit lamp; explain what you're doing and get consent.
Wash hands; have a cotton bud ready.
Ask the patient to look down and keep looking down.
Hold the upper lashes and pull the lid gently down and forward.
Place the bud at the top of the tarsal plate.
Down and round: fold the lid over the bud; hold the lashes against the brow.
Examine with white light, then blue light with fluorescein.

topics.title: Common conditions: blepharitis, MGD, dry eye and conjunctivitis
topics.summary: Most anterior eye problems you'll see are lid margin disease, dry eye and conjunctivitis. Recognise the type from history and signs, give clear self-care advice, and know the red flags that mean referral.
keyPoints: Anterior blepharitis: crusting and collarettes at the lash base (staphylococcal); cylindrical dandruff suggests Demodex.
MGD (posterior blepharitis): capped orifices, thick 'toothpaste' secretions, lid margin telangiectasia; drives evaporative dry eye.
Lid hygiene and warm compresses are the core management for both; it's a chronic condition — set expectations.
Bacterial conjunctivitis: sticky mucopurulent discharge, usually self-limiting; good hygiene; antibiotics if severe or persistent.
Viral (adenoviral) conjunctivitis: watery discharge, follicles, often preauricular lymph node, very contagious; may get subepithelial infiltrates.
Allergic conjunctivitis: itching is key, bilateral, papillae, chemosis; cold compresses, antihistamine/mast cell stabiliser drops.
Red flags: pain, photophobia, reduced vision, unreactive pupil, corneal involvement, recent surgery or CL wear — refer as per College CMGs.
examTraps: Calling every red eye 'conjunctivitis' without checking vision, pupils and cornea.
Forgetting to ask about contact lens wear.
Not telling patients with viral conjunctivitis how contagious it is.

diagram.description: Close-up of the lower lid margin: lashes at the front with crusts and collarettes (anterior blepharitis); meibomian gland orifices behind the grey line, some capped, one expressing thick secretion (MGD); telangiectatic vessels along the margin.

goDeeper.heading: Red eye differential in one minute
goDeeper.body: Conjunctivitis: discharge, vision normal, no pain. Subconjunctival haemorrhage: painless flat red patch. Episcleritis: sectoral redness, mild ache. Scleritis: deep boring pain, violaceous, refer urgently. Anterior uveitis: photophobia, ache, ciliary flush, AC cells. Keratitis: pain, staining, infiltrate. Acute angle closure: severe pain, haloes, hazy cornea, fixed mid-dilated pupil — emergency.

goDeeper.heading: Lid hygiene advice
goDeeper.body: Warm compress (a heated eye mask works well) for 5–10 minutes, then gentle massage towards the lid margin, then clean the lashes with a lid wipe or diluted baby shampoo — daily, long term. Explain that it controls rather than cures, and that it can take weeks to feel better.

goDeeper.heading: College Clinical Management Guidelines
goDeeper.body: The College of Optometrists' CMGs give evidence-based guidance on diagnosis, self-care, what optometrists can manage and when to refer for many anterior eye conditions. They're the go-to reference in UK practice — check them for each condition as you learn it.

cases.question: What's your diagnosis and advice?
cases.modelAnswer: Mixed anterior blepharitis and MGD. Advise daily warm compresses, lid massage and lid cleaning, explain it's chronic and needs ongoing care, consider lubricants for symptoms, and review in a few weeks. Refer if no improvement or if there are atypical features (e.g. loss of lashes, a localised lid lump).

topics.title: The crystalline lens and cataract
topics.summary: How the lens stays clear, how it ages, what cataract does to vision, and when to refer for surgery.
keyPoints: Lens: about 10 mm wide, 4 mm thick, about 15 D; 64% water and 35% protein; index 1.38 (cortex) to 1.40 (nucleus).
Transparency depends on a highly ordered structure; loss comes from protein aggregation, hydration changes, membrane breakdown and cytoskeletal change.
It absorbs UV from 300 to 400 nm; yellowing with age protects the retina.
Symptoms: myopic shift, gradual blur (worse in bright light and for reading), glare, monocular diplopia, haloes.
Types: cortical (63%), nuclear (41%), posterior subcapsular (24%; steroids and uveitis); about 30% mixed.
Refer when it limits quality of life, work or driving (whatever the Snellen acuity) and the patient wants surgery.
Risks: age, UV, smoking, diabetes, cardiovascular and renal disease, dehydration, steroids, low socio-economic status.
examTraps: Using a VA cut-off as the referral criterion: there isn't a fixed one.
Forgetting that nuclear cataract causes a myopic shift.

goDeeper.heading: Phacoemulsification
goDeeper.body: An ultrasonic probe breaks up the nucleus and aspirates it through a small self-sealing incision, leaving the posterior capsule to support the IOL. It's now almost always day-case under local anaesthetic in the UK (about 400,000 NHS operations a year), with lower complication rates and 4–6 weeks' recovery.

goDeeper.heading: Paediatric cataract
goDeeper.body: IOLs can go in from about 4 weeks. The eye is left hyperopic because it will become more myopic as it grows; the other eye is occluded if one eye is operated first. Posterior capsule opacification is common, so a posterior capsulorhexis and limited vitrectomy are done.
